segments.description: Coaches, our next presenter is Gary Cahill. Gary is currently working on the WTA with a number of players and formerly before that he was the Fed and Davis Cup captain for Ireland. Today he's sharing his insights around the importance of a high performing team and how to create one. Coaches, enjoy. Gary, welcome. So good morning everybody and greetings from a very cold blustery Dublin, Ireland. And I would firstly like to say a big thank you to Tennis Australia for inviting me to speak about this conference and particularly to speak about something that I'm really passionate about and that's the whole idea of leadership and in particular leading teams. Just a bit of my background, I've worked in Tennis for 35 years in various capacities. I worked as a Davis Cup captain in Ireland for four years, the Fed Cup captain in Ireland for four years and I travel still and have traveled for almost 30 years on the tour with various players of different levels. But what was interesting for me in my career was I actually ended up pretty much in a leadership job by accident and what happened was I was a coach and suddenly our program started to grow and our training center started to grow and I ended up becoming a leader really without any experience or any qualification in leadership. I had really only coached in my life and I hadn't spent time managing people and in particular managing some of the issues that arise when you're in a leadership capacity, the conflict and

you know trying to build this kind of a team approach with people. So what I'm trying to do with this presentation is basically share some of my experiences. Over the last seven years I've went back and spent quite a lot of time studying these issues. I'm currently doing a PhD, I've completed my master's in a lot of issues around leadership and I'll try to share some of these ideas but you know possibly at the end of it you will have some things that you can reflect on and I hope they'll help you on your journey. But particularly today I'm going to talk about how do you develop a team in this photograph here on the screen is actually the team that I ended up leading and this team is a group of tennis coaches who are working in our national center, also working in our clubs but working in our national center. One of the things I discovered pretty early on is that actually coaching is leadership and you know a lot of the skills that we have as coaches are actually transferable into leading teams. This is a very interesting slide because this scientist John Lyle developed this very very interesting framework where you know he talks about the journey as a coach with players and this is something that I experienced through my career and I know a lot of you are probably experiencing this as well. So when you actually start off as a coach in this first piece here of you know the direct

intervention as John Lyle calls it you know mainly your role is to organize training, schedules, maybe you know organize some competitions but as this player develops you end up where you're dealing with slightly different issues. So for example you know the planning piece becomes more important. There starts to become an administration kind of piece around working with players. You're trying to organize their not just a daily schedule you know the weekly schedule, the people around them and gradually as that grows you end up managing more and more factors. So in this zone here you know you end up managing support services, they're sparring and then eventually it becomes like a strategic planning role where you're managing a full team of people. So it could be from media to like all your support staff to so actually the coaching job the further you go on the road the more it becomes leadership and actually the skills needed change and these are skills as I say you don't learn as a coach a lot of these skills you don't really learn on coaching courses but I think a lot of these skills come from reflection and I'm going to share with you some ideas. So firstly let's start with this what is a high performance team you know and just because you have four or five people working with you are they really a team or what's the difference? So like you can have people that you manage as a team but they can work very separately, they can work individually

you know they may not be accountable to anybody are they really a team or what is a team? Well I think this is a very interesting definition of a team and it comes from Kazun Rakan Smith who you know have done a lot of research in this in this field and they define a team as a small group of people with complementary skills who are committed to a common purpose performance goals and approach for which they hold themselves mutually accountable. Now this for me pretty much sums up what a team is in one definition and the first point to make here is that it's a small group of people and recently I had the opportunity to interview you some CEOs from business and one of them was a very successful business person who manages a massive multinational company and I asked him this question I said well you're a massive leader you have thousands of people working for you how do you manage all these people and he said I don't I'm only able to manage five or six people I said well how does that work? Well I have other people who manage other groups of five or six people but realistically he said I can't manage or lead this number of people you can only lead a small group of people and this is something I have experienced when I was going through my transition that it is really difficult to lead big groups properly a high performance team in my opinion needs to be a small group and I would say that you're talking about a group of yeah five or six people so in your role try to consider

the number of people you're leading is it too many how can you change this so that you're directly working with a smaller group of people now as the leader themselves what is your role and I'm going to show you a very interesting video so here we go to answer that question we set up a hidden camera experiment to see if this woman would stand up at the sound of this tone simply because everyone else is you might be thinking you'd never go along with this or would you after just three beats and without knowing why she's doing it this woman is now conforming perfectly to the group but what happens if we take the group away Elaine please now she's alone the crowd is gone and nobody is watching her except our hidden cameras what do you think she'll do she's now conforming to the rules of the group without them even being there now watch what happens when we introduce another outsider who doesn't know the rules have a seat and they'll be out in just a couple minutes thanks so much think she'll teach the new guy what to do we kept the cameras rolling as more unsuspecting patients arrived and slowly but surely what began as a random rule for this woman has now become the social norm for everyone in this waiting room here to explain what's going on in their brains is Jonah Burke that's amazing I love this video but my advice to you is when you're in the doctor's waiting room next time I wouldn't try it but it's a no but it's a fantastic

video and you know there's there's quite a lot of messages in it but I suppose the first message is that you know your behavior set the tone and people will follow your behaviors in the 8th century BC there was very famous inscription in the Apollo and Delphi which says know thyself and when I think in terms of leading teams it really starts with you and it really starts with your behaviors because as I said your behaviors will influence everything within a team but sometimes these behaviors will not be completely obvious to you you know you could describe it as you know when you you know when you go to the chip shop and smell the chips for the first time that it's really obvious but if you spend a lot of time in the chip shop you actually don't smell the chips anymore and it's a bit like that with behaviors your behaviors become subconscious things that you don't even realize you're doing it but other people pick them up I think it's very important when you start to lead that you firstly reflect on yourself and really understanding what you stand for and this is a really interesting way you know I've explained it but you know a lot of time we start and we try to just change the behavior so okay I'm going to try to do you know something different today but in actual fact you know we we need to go a little bit deeper than that so when we were you know younger and children we we have all these experiences that we get

from our parents and from society people we hang around with these things actually shape our emotions and identity you know these these beliefs shape your behavior these behaviors will influence the results and our behaviors completely influence the people we work with and as I said some of these can be completely subconscious like you know I often find myself you know I say things and I would say Jesus that's exactly how your father used to say it you sound exactly like him but these are these subconscious experiences that come from the past that we don't even really see and I think it's a very good thing to do is to you know ask yourself a little bit about what you actually believe in yourself you know so I think this is a very interesting exercise to do because I do believe as coaches and leaders we should really understand our beliefs our values and our philosophy because you know it's something that we should try on a daily basis to you know to to live to I have a bit of a beef about this idea of you know values now because every training center you go to you see these values plastered on the wall you know I am hardworking I am honest I am you know whatever but actually are these the things that really happen are already just written on a piece of paper for values to really mean something they have to be behaviors they can't be just something that you know we think sounds right but we don't actually we don't

actually live them so this exercise I think is something you should do you should you should sit down and reflect at some point and and ask yourself you know what do you really believe in and how do these beliefs values influence your behaviors so what sort of things do you see on a daily basis from these beliefs and then an interesting question I said well what behaviors do I want my team members to experience from me so you know I'll give you an example uh this is this is uh part of the process that that I went through and you see on the left hand side the beliefs okay well I want to tell the truth you know and sometimes that's not always easy because it can be difficult for people but I want to be honest so what sort of behaviors I want to be honest to the team at all times be honest about their contribution I sometimes need to have the hard conversations so you know the the belief that I'm working from is this value of being honest the behaviors I want to see are are are on the opposite side of the the sheet be there for people outside uh you know and I wanted to be more than just a leader uh I wanted to show actually some genuine interest in the people that that I was leading uh and make time for them not just in the tennis court or you know at meetings but make time outside of the of the of the court but leading a team starts with this and I would encourage you to firstly sit down reflect ask yourself these questions and then you can really

start to work on building your team well this is the first step now secondly and I really like my videos so bear with me uh uh I'm going to show you another video hell why you're a cat a cheshire carry why very cold I just wanted to ask you which way I ought to go well that depends on where do you want to get to oh it really doesn't matter as long as I can it really doesn't matter which way you go you some oh now what the hell has that got to do with leading a team well when you're leading a team you really need to understand what is the purpose of this team and as a leader I have seen so many times within teams where actually this part was missing and without this part a team can't function properly so like this piece Alice well you know which road do I take where do you want to go well if you don't know where you're going to go then any road can take you there and it's a bit like that with leading teams you need to be very clear about exactly what you're trying to achieve so you know in a tennis context is it you know I want to improve the training is it that I want to bring in more members is it that what exactly is the purpose of this team and all team members need to have a commitment to this purpose because this purpose develops the direction of momentum and actually it develops the commitment from people and the best teams actually invest a lot of time and effort exploring and shaping

the agreement on what exactly this purpose is and only then can you start to actually really plan how the team are going to get there and I like to think of it like this so when you're leading a team you have to start with this intention what is it we are really trying to achieve do we all agree with this are we all clear on it if we don't agree on it let's talk about it let's let's see what we do agree on and you start with the intention but the intention but the intention determines all the attention so when you have a very clear intention then you can start building your blocks of attention so for example you know if I know my intention is to do x then these blocks are the blocks that I would put in around my attention so for example I'm trying to improve the quality of the training in our programs well one of the intentions is we're going to actually design a complete annual plan we're going to improve our lesson planning for our athletes we're going to provide more individual lessons but the point is that they have to work to a very clear intention and this intention should be obvious daily within your training and within your training center within your team so my second bit of advice to you when you're leading teams is to ask yourself these questions what are we trying to achieve as a team so what would that look like if we actually achieved it so what would success look like if we actually achieved this goal and then this is a very important question

what contribution can each member of this team make to this goal and that's where you get into your team members having specific roles and specific goals within this objective and I think that this process is really your starting point to build a high performance team so this little reflection piece here again I would encourage you to sit think through this and be very clear about these three questions so this isn't a really nice pyramid of you know how to build a high performance team and this is by Len Keone who wrote this book called the five behaviors of a cohesive team it's this functional team behaviors dysfunctional team and it's a it's a really really really nice model so basically what Len Keone says is that you know that the whole team is built around trust and you know if if a team don't trust each other they're going to be really afraid to communicate honestly openly and and they're going to end up hiding a lot of their real thoughts and feelings you know and and this this really makes it impossible to build a team so as leaders we have to be very conscious firstly of of actually how do we kind of build this team from trust because the rest of the pyramid will not happen unless you have the trust because you know a conflict is very important and I'll speak about that again in a minute but without the trust piece in the beginning you won't have conflict and then you're unlikely to have

the commitment you're unlikely to have everybody you know being accountable they don't trust each other and it will affect your results so how do you build trust it's a it's a really you know and I think the expression that it takes a long time to build it and it can be destroyed very quickly is really apt because trust takes time and I have three tips that I think help to build trust and and the first tip is you know trust to a certain extent comes from showing some vulnerability within your team now I'm just going to have to plug in my charger so just one second apologies for that so yeah as I was saying trust it's difficult it takes it takes time to build but it's easy to destroy it and it can be destroyed very quickly but to build trust I think it really helps for a leader to be honest but show some vulnerability and you know there's nothing worse than a leader who is not prepared to admit when they're wrong so it helps sometimes to say I screwed up or I need help or because nobody's perfect and and sharing this kind of vulnerability we know scientifically actually helps to build trust and obviously you know to be very honest with people and this can be difficult but you know you have to try it all times to be honest but particularly I think to see things true if you tell people things I think it's really important to see them true there's nothing worse than a leader who promises things and doesn't actually doesn't actually follow true in them and then

I think as well to look for things in common you know I was looking off that not just did my team have the common love of tennis but we love certain things outside of tennis so we like to say football team is to go through football matches you have you have more in common with people sometimes than you think but to try and find those common themes I think can be really interesting you know one thing we used to do as a team was we used to you know go to different activities on a regular basis and not like a kind of a cheesy team day but you know things that we knew we liked that was you know outside of our environment and I think that really really helps to to build this trust piece the conflict is actually really important in a team and I think that without conflict it's actually quite hard to grow and I love this quote conflict is growth trying to happen you know there's nothing worse than pushing important issues under the carpet because they just fester and it's a it's a really good sign of a trusting team when they can have these hard honest conversations walk away from it and grow from it but how do you kind of build this well I think you have to make it known to the team that actually there is such thing as constructive conflict and you encourage it in my team I had one member who you know was always the devil's advocate and you know whenever you know we discussed plans this team member

always had issues always found a negative piece in the plan and this used to piss off quite a few of the team members but in actual fact we started to you know look at it as a as a really good thing and you need that kind of diversity within your team that somebody is willing to ask the tough questions and we should be encouraging that rather than not encouraging this kind of conflict and I'm conscious of the time just some basic tips when it comes to you know this idea of kind of build and trust and you know I think given responsibility is is really important that you're willing to trust the people to do things there's nothing worse than working for a micromanager you have to give people the freedom to take responsibility and I think that helps to grow trust we used to play this game two truths and a lie and basically where I do it sometimes with the players where you have to tell two things that are true about yourself that probably people wouldn't know and one that's a lie and people have to guess which one is a lie and it's amazing what you find out about people from from this simple exercise and I suppose the other tip being Irish is yeah just going for a beer with with the team or going out with the team and just getting away from the sport I'm at my end here and I just I just show you finally you know some of my basic philosophies as a you know as a leader yeah I'm not asking you to copy these but

you know when I reflected on my beliefs and values and philosophy you know I I also you know taught true well how do I actually want to be when I lead and you know I wanted to be a coach help my team to set development goals not just about the daily practice how are they going to get better I always believe in giving the team autonomy let them let them have responsibility they'll grow from it they'll trust you more and they'll enjoy it more we're part of something bigger understand your purpose constructive challenge is a fantastic thing and these constructive challenges should always be left at the door when you walk out the door they're over and trust bonds a team show yourself to people let them know who the real person is so finally I just like to say thank you to tennis Australia again for inviting me I hope this helps you but you know I hope it helps you just at least reflect and if anybody wants to get in touch with me at any stage I'm happy to share my email address with tennis Australia so again thank you very much for the opportunity and enjoy the journey bye
